extracted.intended_audience: poets, writers, public speakers, and readers interested in literary craft and voice
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and aesthetic guidance on cultivating the human voice (for reading, speaking, and poetic utterance), the character of American poetry, and related choices about subjectivity and public performance. Covers physiological basis of voice, aims for poetry, lecturing style, and use of personal material.

rubrics_metrics.name: The human voice as cultivated growth
rubrics_metrics.description: “The human voice is a cultivation or form'd growth on a fair native foundation. This foundation probably exists in nine cases out of ten.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize that a good voice usually rests on an innate physiological foundation which must be cultivated; teachers and elocution help are secondary to developing the natural vocal organ. The author stresses beginning with the native gift and cultivating it rather than manufacturing a voice from scratch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of physiology in the grand voice
rubrics_metrics.description: “To me the grand voice is mainly physiological--(by which I by no means ignore the mental help, but wish to keep the emphasis where it belongs.)”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or developing a speaking/reading voice, prioritize physiological factors (timbre, breath, vocal power) over purely intellectual or rhetorical manipulations. Mental qualities contribute, but the core power and beauty come from physical vocal quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timbre (quality) as the soul-touching element
rubrics_metrics.description: “Beyond all other power and beauty, there is something in the quality and power of the right voice (_timbre_ the schools call it) that touches the soul, the abysms.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess voice by its timbre — the unique quality that can move listeners profoundly. Examples of exemplary timbre are given (Alboni, Elias Hicks, Father Taylor, Bettini, Fanny Kemble, Booth) to show that timbre, more than style or doctrine, often defines greatness in vocal utterance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice as vehicle for reviving philosophy and poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: “I sometimes wonder whether the best philosophy and poetry... perhaps waits to be rous'd out yet, or suggested, by the perfect physiological human voice.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the voice not merely as delivery but as a creative instrument that can awaken or suggest new depths of thought and poetry; great vocalization may itself catalyze fresh philosophical or poetic insights.

rubrics_metrics.name: American poetry should be spiritual and democratic
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Old World... is the region of the poetry of concrete and real things... But the New World (America) is the region of the future, and its poetry must be spiritual and democratic.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or judging American verse, value work that looks forward — emphasizing spiritual/democratic themes rather than merely the past, the esthetic, or mythological concerns of Old World models. The poet should aim to reflect democratic spirit and expanded modern 'spirituality.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution and science as criteria for future poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: “Evolution is not the rule in Nature... but in Verse. ... Then science, the final critic of all, has the casting vote for future poetry.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor poetic approaches that acknowledge and incorporate contemporary understanding (evolutionary thought, scientific outlook); expect future poetry to be judged (in part) by its consonance with modern scientific/spiritual comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not write primarily for the public or established authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: “No free and original and lofty-soaring poem... can possibly be fulfill'd by any writer who has largely in his thought _the public_--or the question, What will established literature... say about it?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid composing with the main aim of pleasing current public taste, critics, or established literary authorities. Such an orientation is presented as an anti-pattern that inhibits originality and loftiness of ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model on Nature (not the garden) when choosing aesthetic examples
rubrics_metrics.description: “As far as I have sought any, not the best laid out garden or parterre has been my model--but Nature has been. ... Besides the gardens are well represented in poetry; while Nature... little if at all.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer Nature (broad, untended, elemental experience) as the model and source for poetic material and style rather than cultivated, conventional 'garden' examples. This choice supports originality and freshness in poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to arouse the soul's eligibility rather than feed esthetic palates
rubrics_metrics.description: “I have never so much cared to feed the esthetic or intellectual palates--but if I could arouse from its slumbers that eligibility in every soul for its own true exercise!”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value work that seeks to awaken readers' inner capacities and participation rather than merely pleasing critics or offering ornate aesthetic display. The highest aim is to stimulate genuine soul-exercise and democratic engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of personal/autobiographic material is legitimate
rubrics_metrics.description: “I will not reject any theme or subject because the treatment is too personal. ... it is mainly autobiographic, and even egotistic after all--which I finally accept, and am contented so.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept autobiographical or personally 'egotistic' material as valid subject matter. Authors should not dismiss themes simply because they are personal; candid personal treatment can be an important creative approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust ambitions and production to bodily/temporal limits
rubrics_metrics.description: “If this little volume betrays...a weakening hand, and decrepitude, remember it is knit together out of accumulated sickness... The resolve to keep up, and on, and to add a remnant... have produced it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing work while physically limited or late in life, be honest about constraints, accept smaller or fragmentary forms, and value the contribution of failing powers rather than forcing unsuitable ambitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture/reading should be concise and modest in length
rubrics_metrics.description: “I intend to go up and down the land (in moderation,) seeking whom I may devour, with lectures, and reading of my own poems--short pulls, however--never exceeding an hour.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For public readings and lectures, prefer short, concentrated performances (‘short pulls’) and avoid overly long addresses; moderation in touring and concise delivery are recommended for effectiveness and sustainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective oratory: voice, style, and spontaneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of Ingersoll's speech: voice 'low enough and not too low,' style 'easy, rather colloquial,' delivered 'altogether without notes,' 'sometimes markedly impassion'd, once or twice humorous.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate or craft spoken addresses for a natural, well-modulated voice, conversational style, emotional conviction, occasional humor, and minimal reliance on notes. Physical presence and magnetism (voice and persona) are key to admirable oratory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sometimes presence is better than a prepared speech
rubrics_metrics.description: At the complimentary dinner Whitman: 'My friends, though announced to give an address, there is no such intention... I have obey'd the command to come and look at you, for a minute, and show myself, face to face;' he declines speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that in some public/social contexts, silent presence or a brief personal showing may be more appropriate and effective than delivering a formal speech. Avoid forcing rhetoric where simple presence suffices.
